entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: A yellow-orange colouring based on curcuminoids from turmeric.
entries.expanded_summary: A yellow-orange colouring based on curcuminoids from turmeric. It is a concentrated colour preparation rather than simply ground turmeric spice.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by extracting and refining the colour-rich compounds from turmeric rhizomes.
entries.fact_1_copy: Curcumin is the best-known yellow pigment in turmeric.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to give foods a yellow to orange colour.

entries.tile_summary: Amaranth is a synthetic food colour designed to give a strong, consistent red to reddish-purple shade.
entries.expanded_summary: Amaranth is a synthetic food colour designed to give a strong, consistent red to reddish-purple shade. It is a manufactured dye rather than a colour extracted from a food or plant.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by controlled chemical synthesis and purified to food-additive specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used for a stable red to reddish-purple colour in foods and drinks.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Copper chlorophyll and chlorophyllin complexes are greener, more stable derivatives of plant chlorophyll.
entries.expanded_summary: Copper chlorophyll and chlorophyllin complexes are greener, more stable derivatives of plant chlorophyll. Copper is introduced into the pigment structure to improve colour stability.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with chlorophyll from plant material, then is processed to replace the central magnesium with copper; chlorophyllin forms are further modified to improve water solubility.
entries.fact_1_copy: The starting pigment is natural chlorophyll, but the food colour is chemically modified for stability.
entries.fact_2_copy: Provides a more stable green colour than unmodified chlorophyll.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with an existing material — natural or manufactured — and deliberately transforms it using processes such as heating, roasting, oxidation, hydrolysis, neutralisation or other controlled treatment. The starting material can be materially changed in colour, structure or food-technology behaviour.
entries.tile_summary: Caramel IV is a brown colouring made by controlled heat treatment of sugars or other food-grade carbohydrates.
entries.expanded_summary: Caramel IV is a brown colouring made by controlled heat treatment of sugars or other food-grade carbohydrates. It is a colour ingredient, not simply the caramel made when sugar is browned in a kitchen.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by heated carbohydrates in the presence of both ammonium and sulphite compounds, creating a complex mixture of brown colour compounds.
entries.fact_1_copy: Ammonia-sulphite caramel.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to give foods and drinks brown to dark-brown colour.
entries.evidence_copy: Europe's food-safety authority found no evidence that Caramel IV damages genes or causes cancer. It also assessed expected exposure to a manufacturing by-product called 4-methylimidazole and found no concern when the colour met its specification limits. The finding therefore depends on control of the manufactured colour and its by-products; it does not identify Caramel IV itself as a human carcinogen.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: EFSA reviews safety of caramel colours (2011)

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Paprika oleoresin is a concentrated red-orange colour extract from paprika peppers.
entries.expanded_summary: Paprika oleoresin is a concentrated red-orange colour extract from paprika peppers. Its colour comes mainly from carotenoids such as capsanthin and capsorubin.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by extracting and refining colour-rich material from dried Capsicum peppers.
entries.fact_1_copy: Made from paprika-type peppers rather than from synthetic colour molecules.
entries.fact_2_copy: Provides orange to red colouring and may retain some pepper-derived components.

entries.tile_summary: Kryptoxanthin is a carotenoid-family pigment associated with yellow-orange colouring.
entries.expanded_summary: Kryptoxanthin is a carotenoid-family pigment associated with yellow-orange colouring. It belongs to the same broad natural pigment family as beta-carotene and lutein.
entries.source_preparation_copy: This carotenoid occurs in natural biological sources; commercial food-colour preparations may depend on the approved source and manufacturing specification.
entries.fact_1_copy: A xanthophyll carotenoid.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for yellow-orange colouring where permitted.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Saffron colour preparations are based on pigments such as crocin and crocetin from saffron.
entries.expanded_summary: Saffron colour preparations are based on pigments such as crocin and crocetin from saffron. These carotenoid-related compounds give saffron its characteristic golden colour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Obtained from saffron plant material and refined to concentrate the colouring compounds.
entries.fact_1_copy: Saffron comes from the stigmas of Crocus sativus flowers.
entries.fact_2_copy: Provides yellow to golden colouring.

entries.tile_summary: Tannins are a broad family of plant polyphenols with astringent properties.
entries.expanded_summary: Tannins are a broad family of plant polyphenols with astringent properties. Tannic acid is a more defined tannin-rich material historically obtained from plant galls and other tannin-rich sources.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Obtained by extracting and refining tannin-rich plant material.
entries.fact_1_copy: Tannins occur naturally in tea, grapes, many fruits, bark and other plant tissues.
entries.fact_2_copy: Tannins can contribute dryness or astringency as well as technological effects.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: This preservative helps acidic foods and drinks last longer by slowing the growth of yeasts, moulds and some bacteria.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium benzoate (211) helps preserve acidic foods and drinks, including some soft drinks, fruit drinks and sauces. It slows the growth of yeasts, moulds and certain bacteria. It is the sodium salt of benzoic acid, and its effectiveness depends on the product's acidity and formulation.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising benzoic acid with a sodium source, giving a water-soluble benzoate salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: A sodium salt in the benzoate family, commonly used as a food preservative.
entries.fact_2_copy: Works especially well in acidic foods and drinks; the formulation also matters.
entries.evidence_copy:
An Australian total-diet study published in 2005 estimated that some high-consuming young children could exceed the acceptable daily intake (ADI) for benzoates, with drinks a major contributor. Average estimated exposures were below half the ADI. The ADI includes a substantial safety margin; exceeding it does not, by itself, demonstrate harm.

In some beverages containing benzoates and vitamin C, small amounts of benzene can form, particularly with heat or light. FDA monitoring found that most tested beverages had no detectable benzene or less than 5 parts per billion. Some higher findings led manufacturers to reformulate. Formation depends on the beverage's formulation and storage conditions, not on E211 alone.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: Australia and New Zealand food regulator: 21st Australian Total Diet Study (2005 report; current FSANZ archive)
entries.evidence_source_2_link_label: United States food regulator: Questions and answers on benzene in soft drinks and other beverages (current FDA page)

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Sodium sulphite is a sodium sulphite salt that can release sulphur dioxide-related preserving species in food.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium sulphite is a sodium sulphite salt that can release sulphur dioxide-related preserving species in food.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by reacting sulphur dioxide with a sodium alkali and crystallising the salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Part of the sulphite preservative family.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for preservation, antioxidant action and browning control.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Nisin is an antimicrobial peptide produced by certain strains of Lactococcus lactis, a bacterium associated with dairy fermentation.
entries.expanded_summary: Nisin is an antimicrobial peptide produced by certain strains of Lactococcus lactis, a bacterium associated with dairy fermentation. It is used to inhibit particular spoilage and food-poisoning bacteria.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by controlled fermentation with nisin-producing bacteria, then recovered and standardised for food use.
entries.fact_1_copy: A small protein-like peptide, not a conventional synthetic preservative molecule.
entries.fact_2_copy: Especially useful against some Gram-positive bacteria and bacterial spores.

entries.tile_summary: Acetic acid is the acid responsible for vinegar's characteristic sourness and sharp smell.
entries.expanded_summary: Acetic acid is the acid responsible for vinegar's characteristic sourness and sharp smell. As an additive it can acidify food, help control pH and contribute preservative effects.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Food-grade acetic acid can be produced by fermentation of ethanol or by chemical manufacture, then purified to the required concentration.
entries.fact_1_copy: Vinegar is a dilute food solution of acetic acid made by fermentation.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as an acid, acidity regulator and preservative depending on the product.

entries.source_profile_definition: The same additive identity can legitimately be made from different starting materials or by different manufacturing routes. The additive code alone therefore cannot tell you one reliable origin.
entries.tile_summary: Propionic acid is a short-chain organic acid that also occurs naturally in some fermented foods.
entries.expanded_summary: Propionic acid is a short-chain organic acid that also occurs naturally in some fermented foods. It is particularly useful for slowing mould growth in bakery products.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial propionic acid is mainly produced by chemical manufacture, although propionic acid is also made biologically by fermentation.
entries.fact_1_copy: Propionic-acid bacteria produce it in foods such as Swiss-style cheese.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a preservative, especially against moulds.

entries.tile_summary: Fumaric acid is an organic acid that occurs naturally in small amounts in living organisms and some plants.
entries.expanded_summary: Fumaric acid is an organic acid that occurs naturally in small amounts in living organisms and some plants. It has a strong acidifying effect and low water solubility.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Food-grade fumaric acid is generally manufactured by chemical processes and purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used as an acid and acidity regulator.
entries.fact_2_copy: Its relatively low solubility can make its acid effect persist differently from more soluble acids.

entries.tile_summary: Alpha-tocopherol is a form of vitamin E and a lipid-soluble antioxidant.
entries.expanded_summary: Alpha-tocopherol is a form of vitamin E and a lipid-soluble antioxidant. It can be used to help protect fats and oils from oxidation.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Food-grade alpha-tocopherol may be isolated from vegetable-oil sources or manufactured as a defined tocopherol preparation, depending on the form.
entries.fact_1_copy: Alpha-tocopherol is the biologically prominent form of vitamin E.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as an antioxidant in fat-containing foods.

entries.tile_summary: Octyl gallate is an ester of gallic acid designed to work as an antioxidant in fats and oils.
entries.expanded_summary: Octyl gallate is an ester of gallic acid designed to work as an antioxidant in fats and oils. The octyl group makes the molecule more compatible with fatty ingredients than gallic acid itself.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by chemically esterifying gallic acid with the corresponding octyl alcohol and purifying the product.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used to slow oxidative rancidity in fats and oils.
entries.fact_2_copy: Built from gallic-acid chemistry but manufactured as a more fat-soluble ester.

entries.tile_summary: Butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT) is a synthetic phenolic antioxidant.
entries.expanded_summary: Butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT) is a synthetic phenolic antioxidant. It is used in small amounts to slow oxidative rancidity and protect flavour or shelf life in fat-containing foods.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by controlled organic chemical synthesis and purified to food-additive specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: Helps protect fats and oils from oxidation.

entries.tile_summary: Magnesium lactate is the magnesium salt of lactic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Magnesium lactate is the magnesium salt of lactic acid. It keeps the familiar lactic-acid chemistry but in a less acidic salt form.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising lactic acid — commonly produced by fermentation of sugars — with a magnesium-containing base.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from lactic acid, the acid associated with many fermented foods.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the salt, can regulate acidity, retain moisture, firm texture or support preservation.

entries.tile_summary: Sodium tartrate is a sodium salt of tartaric acid, the fruit acid closely associated with grapes and wine.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium tartrate is a sodium salt of tartaric acid, the fruit acid closely associated with grapes and wine.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by neutralising purified tartaric acid or recovering and refining naturally formed tartrate salts from food-processing streams.
entries.fact_1_copy: Built from tartaric acid chemistry.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for acidity control, buffering, stabilisation or raising-agent chemistry depending on the salt.

entries.entry_title: Calcium phosphate, dibasic or calcium hydrogen phosphate (341)
entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Calcium phosphates are a family of calcium salts of phosphoric acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Calcium phosphates are a family of calcium salts of phosphoric acid. Schedule 8 groups several mono-, di- or tribasic forms under the same additive number.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by reacting purified phosphoric acid with calcium-containing mineral or chemical bases and controlling the degree of neutralisation.
entries.fact_1_copy: Different phosphate forms have different acidity, solubility and buffering behaviour.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the form, phosphates can regulate acidity, act in raising systems, stabilise texture or bind water.
entries.evidence_copy: Although 341 also contains calcium, Europe's food-safety authority assessed its phosphate as part of total phosphorus from the whole diet. The phosphate group was not considered likely to damage genes or cause cancer, but some European exposure estimates for infants and children were above the group safety value. This does not make an individual food containing 341 unsafe; the assessment adds natural phosphorus, phosphate additives and supplements across the diet.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of phosphoric acid and phosphates E338-341, E343, E450-452 (2019)

entries.expanded_summary: Calcium malate is a calcium salt of malic acid, the tart fruit acid associated with apples and many other fruits.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising purified malic acid with a calcium-containing base.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from malic acid chemistry.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used mainly for acidity control, buffering or mineral delivery depending on the salt.

entries.tile_summary: Succinic acid is a small organic acid that occurs naturally in living cells as part of energy metabolism.
entries.expanded_summary: Succinic acid is a small organic acid that occurs naturally in living cells as part of energy metabolism. Food-grade succinic acid is used for acidity and flavour effects.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial succinic acid can be produced by chemical synthesis or increasingly by fermentation of renewable carbohydrate starting materials.
entries.fact_1_copy: Succinate is part of the normal citric-acid cycle in cells.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as an acid, acidity regulator or flavour-related ingredient.

entries.tile_summary: Ferric ammonium citrate is an iron-containing citrate complex rather than a single simple salt.
entries.expanded_summary: Ferric ammonium citrate is an iron-containing citrate complex rather than a single simple salt. It combines iron with citrate and ammonium in a water-compatible form.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Prepared by reacting iron compounds, citric acid and ammonia under controlled conditions and drying the resulting complex.
entries.fact_1_copy: It is a coordination mixture/complex, not simply iron metal or plain citric acid.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used where iron and citrate chemistry provides the desired technological effect.

entries.tile_summary: Ammonium alginate is the ammonium salt of alginic acid, part of a family of gel-forming carbohydrates obtained from brown seaweed.
entries.expanded_summary: Ammonium alginate is the ammonium salt of alginic acid, part of a family of gel-forming carbohydrates obtained from brown seaweed.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Brown seaweed is washed, extracted and processed to isolate alginate; the required acid or salt form is then purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Alginate is a structural polysaccharide in brown algae.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to thicken, stabilise or form gels depending on the form and food.

entries.expanded_summary: Arabinogalactan, also called larch gum, is a highly branched soluble plant carbohydrate obtained mainly from larch wood.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Extracted from larch wood with water, then purified, concentrated and dried.
entries.fact_1_copy: A natural polysaccharide in larch trees.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for stabilising, bulking or fibre-like technological functions depending on the product.

entries.expanded_summary: Karaya gum is a gum exuded from Sterculia trees. It is a plant-derived hydrocolloid used to manage texture and water in foods.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Collected or extracted from Sterculia tree exudate, then cleaned, milled and/or purified to food-grade specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: A high-molecular-weight carbohydrate rather than a simple sugar.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for thickening, stabilising or controlling texture.

entries.tile_summary: Polyoxyethylene (40) stearate is an emulsifier made by combining stearic-acid chemistry with a polyoxyethylene chain.
entries.expanded_summary: Polyoxyethylene (40) stearate is an emulsifier made by combining stearic-acid chemistry with a polyoxyethylene chain. It is purpose-built to help oil- and water-based ingredients mix.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by reacting stearic-acid-derived material with ethylene oxide under controlled conditions, then purifying the product.
entries.fact_1_copy: Acts as an emulsifier and stabiliser.
entries.fact_2_copy: The fatty-acid component can originate from fats or oils, but the final ingredient is chemically manufactured.

entries.expanded_summary: Ammonium salts of phosphatidic acid are emulsifiers based on phospholipid-like molecules related to the components of lecithin.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced from phosphatidic-acid-rich material derived from edible fats or oils, followed by ammonium neutralisation and controlled processing.
entries.fact_1_copy: Helps manage mixtures of fat, cocoa solids and other ingredients, especially in confectionery.

entries.tile_summary: Yeast mannoproteins are carbohydrate-protein molecules from the outer cell wall of yeast.
entries.expanded_summary: Yeast mannoproteins are carbohydrate-protein molecules from the outer cell wall of yeast. In wine and some other applications they can influence stability and mouthfeel.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Recovered from yeast cell-wall material produced during yeast growth or fermentation, then purified and standardised.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from yeast rather than from a synthetic polymer.
entries.fact_2_copy: Can help stabilise colloids or tartrate behaviour and influence texture depending on the application.

entries.tile_summary: Methyl ethyl cellulose is a chemically modified form of plant cellulose.
entries.expanded_summary: Methyl ethyl cellulose is a chemically modified form of plant cellulose. Introducing methyl and ethyl groups changes cellulose from an insoluble plant fibre into a material with useful thickening, film-forming or stabilising behaviour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with purified plant cellulose, which is reacted under controlled conditions to introduce methyl and ethyl groups; the product is then washed and purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant cellulose, commonly from wood pulp or cotton-derived material.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a thickener, stabiliser, film former or texture modifier depending on the derivative.

entries.expanded_summary: Citric and fatty acid esters of glycerol are emulsifiers made by adding citric acid-derived groups to mono- and diglyceride-type fat molecules. The modification changes how the molecules interact with dough, fat and water.

entries.fact_1_copy: Built on glycerol and fatty acids, the same broad building blocks found in edible fats.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as emulsifiers and texture/process aids, with some forms particularly important in bakery applications.

entries.expanded_summary: Calcium chloride is a highly soluble calcium salt.

entries.fact_1_copy: Used as a firming agent, flour treatment material, acidity regulator or calcium source; in tofu it can act as a coagulant.

entries.expanded_summary: Calcium oxide, also known as quicklime, is an inorganic alkaline material. It reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide and can be used for pH control and processing.

entries.fact_1_copy: A strongly or moderately basic calcium-containing compound used for processing rather than flavour.
entries.fact_2_copy: Its technical name can sound severe because concentrated material is reactive; food use is controlled and application-specific.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Amorphous silicon dioxide is a finely divided form of silica.
entries.expanded_summary: Amorphous silicon dioxide is a finely divided form of silica.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced from purified silica/silicate starting materials by precipitation, gel formation or thermal processes.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used mainly as an anticaking agent and carrier because its porous particles absorb moisture and keep powders free-flowing.
entries.evidence_copy: Europe's food-safety authority assessed 551 using both conventional and nanoscale approaches because some primary particles and aggregates can be extremely small. It concluded that very little is likely to reach the bloodstream and found no safety concern for any age group, including infants under 16 weeks. It separately recommended tighter limits for metal impurities in the food-grade specification.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of silicon dioxide E551 (2024)

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Bentonite is a swelling clay dominated by montmorillonite minerals.
entries.expanded_summary: Bentonite is a swelling clay dominated by montmorillonite minerals.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Mined from natural clay deposits, then dried, milled and purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used for clarification, adsorption or processing; it can bind proteins and suspended material.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium gluconate is the potassium salt of gluconic acid, an acid made by oxidising glucose.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium gluconate is the potassium salt of gluconic acid, an acid made by oxidising glucose. The gluconate part is highly water-compatible and can bind minerals.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced from fermentation/oxidation-derived gluconic acid followed by neutralisation with a potassium-containing source.
entries.fact_1_copy: Glucose-derived gluconic acid.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the mineral, used for mineral delivery, acidity control, sequestration, colour stabilisation or processing.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Monosodium L-glutamate / MSG is the sodium salt of glutamic acid, the amino acid associated with umami taste.
entries.expanded_summary: Monosodium L-glutamate / MSG is the sodium salt of glutamic acid, the amino acid associated with umami taste. MSG is the best-known glutamate flavour enhancer.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Glutamic acid is commonly produced by microbial fermentation of sugars or starch hydrolysates, then neutralised with a sodium source to make the salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Glutamate occurs naturally in foods including tomatoes, mushrooms, seaweed and aged cheeses.
entries.fact_2_copy: The glutamate ion provides savoury umami taste.
entries.fact_3_copy: Added glutamate and naturally occurring glutamate are the same glutamate ion once dissolved in food.
entries.evidence_copy: Australia and New Zealand's food regulator found no convincing evidence that MSG causes serious systemic illness or is a significant asthma trigger. A small number of people may experience short-lived symptoms after a large amount in one meal, particularly without other food. Added MSG must be declared as MSG or 621; naturally occurring glutamate and glutamate in ingredients such as yeast extract are not labelled as added MSG.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: Australia and New Zealand food regulator: MSG in food (updated 2025-11-26)

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Disodium 5′-inosinate is the disodium salt of a inosine nucleotide.
entries.expanded_summary: Disodium 5′-inosinate is the disodium salt of a inosine nucleotide. These nucleotide flavour enhancers strongly boost savoury taste, especially when used together with glutamate.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial food-grade nucleotide salts are commonly produced from microbial fermentation or enzymatic processing of biological nucleotide material, then purified and converted to the sodium salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Guanylate and inosinate can amplify umami far more strongly when combined with glutamate than when used alone.
entries.fact_2_copy: Related nucleotide compounds occur naturally in foods and cells.
entries.fact_3_copy: Used as flavour enhancers in savoury foods.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Polydimethylsiloxane (dimethylpolysiloxane) is a silicone polymer used in tiny amounts to control foam.
entries.expanded_summary: Polydimethylsiloxane (dimethylpolysiloxane) is a silicone polymer used in tiny amounts to control foam. Its chain is built from alternating silicon and oxygen atoms with methyl groups attached.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured from purified silicon-derived chemical intermediates through controlled polymerisation.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used mainly as an antifoaming agent during processing.
entries.fact_2_copy: A silicone polymer — chemically different from elemental silicon or silica minerals.

entries.source_profile_definition: The same additive identity can legitimately be made from different starting materials or by different manufacturing routes. The additive code alone therefore cannot tell you one reliable origin.
entries.tile_summary: L-cysteine hydrochloride is a salt of L-cysteine, a sulphur-containing amino acid found naturally in proteins.
entries.expanded_summary: L-cysteine hydrochloride is a salt of L-cysteine, a sulphur-containing amino acid found naturally in proteins. In food processing it is particularly known for changing dough properties.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Modern food-grade L-cysteine can be produced by microbial fermentation or other controlled manufacturing routes, then converted to the hydrochloride salt and purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Cysteine is a normal amino-acid component of many proteins.
entries.fact_2_copy: Can act as a flour treatment agent by modifying disulphide bonds in dough proteins.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number does not by itself disclose the manufacturing source, so source-specific dietary concerns require product or supplier information.

entries.source_profile_definition: A purified gas used in or around food. It may dissolve into the product, displace oxygen in a package, create bubbles or foam, or act as a propellant.
entries.tile_summary: Octafluorocyclobutane is a fully fluorinated cyclic gas.
entries.expanded_summary: Octafluorocyclobutane is a fully fluorinated cyclic gas.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by controlled fluorochemical synthesis and purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used as a specialised propellant or packaging gas in limited applications.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for its gas/pressure properties rather than as a conventional solid or liquid ingredient.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Alitame is a high-intensity sweetener built from amino-acid-derived components.
entries.expanded_summary: Alitame is a high-intensity sweetener built from amino-acid-derived components. Its peptide-like structure is engineered for very strong sweetness.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by controlled chemical synthesis from amino-acid-derived building blocks and purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Thousands of times sweeter than sucrose, so only very small amounts are needed.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as an intense sweetener rather than a bulk sugar replacement.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Lactitol is a sugar alcohol made from lactose, the natural sugar in milk.
entries.expanded_summary: Lactitol is a sugar alcohol made from lactose, the natural sugar in milk. Hydrogenation changes lactose into a less-sweet polyol used for bulk and texture.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by catalytic hydrogenation of lactose, followed by purification and crystallisation.
entries.fact_1_copy: Lactose, the milk sugar.
entries.fact_2_copy: Milder than sucrose.
entries.fact_3_copy: Used as a bulk sweetener, texture ingredient and humectant.

entries.source_profile_definition: A protein that performs a specific biological job. Food enzymes may be extracted from plants or animals, or produced by microorganisms grown by fermentation. They speed up reactions such as breaking starch, protein or fat into smaller components.
entries.tile_summary: Proteases such as papain, bromelain and ficin are protein-cutting enzymes.
entries.expanded_summary: Proteases such as papain, bromelain and ficin are protein-cutting enzymes. These named examples come from papaya, pineapple and fig-family plants respectively.
entries.source_preparation_copy: The named plant proteases are extracted and purified from their source plants; other protease preparations can also be produced by microbial fermentation depending on the approved enzyme.
entries.fact_1_copy: Papain — papaya; bromelain — pineapple; ficin — fig latex.
entries.fact_2_copy: Break proteins into smaller peptides and amino-acid fragments.
entries.fact_3_copy: Used for tenderising, clarifying, modifying dough/protein texture and other processing purposes.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Dextrin / roasted starch is starch that has been dry-heated so some long starch chains break and rearrange.
entries.expanded_summary: Dextrin / roasted starch is starch that has been dry-heated so some long starch chains break and rearrange. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes dry roasting, often with small amounts of acid, without adding a new major functional group, followed by washing and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
entries.fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

entries.tile_summary: Monostarch phosphate is starch carrying phosphate groups on individual starch chains.
entries.expanded_summary: Monostarch phosphate is starch carrying phosphate groups on individual starch chains. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes phosphorylation, followed by washing and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
entries.fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

entries.tile_summary: Hydroxypropyl starch is starch carrying hydroxypropyl groups.
entries.expanded_summary: Hydroxypropyl starch is starch carrying hydroxypropyl groups. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes hydroxypropylation, followed by washing and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
entries.fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Propylene glycol is a small, colourless liquid that mixes readily with water and is useful for carrying flavours, colours and other ingredients.
entries.expanded_summary: Propylene glycol is a small, colourless liquid that mixes readily with water and is useful for carrying flavours, colours and other ingredients. It also helps retain moisture.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by hydration of propylene oxide or related chemical routes, then highly purified for food use.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used as a solvent/carrier, humectant and texture-related ingredient.
entries.fact_2_copy: It is chemically different from ethylene glycol, the toxic compound associated with automotive antifreeze.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Mushroom chitosan is a natural fungal cell-wall polymer sourced from Agaricus bisporus mushrooms.
entries.expanded_summary: Mushroom chitosan is a natural fungal cell-wall polymer sourced from Agaricus bisporus mushrooms. Unlike conventional chitosan, which is often made from crustacean shells, this specified ingredient is mushroom-derived.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Obtained from Agaricus bisporus fungal material and processed to isolate a chitosan/chitin-beta-glucan co-polymer preparation.
entries.fact_1_copy: Mushroom rather than shellfish.
entries.fact_2_copy: A natural co-polymer containing chitin/chitosan-related and beta-glucan components.
entries.fact_3_copy: FSANZ lists this additive by name without a numeric additive code.
